tldr: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis and released the proof as a 14-part Lean archive. It is unverified: nobody has yet replayed the full proof, and a rival 'all human' GRH proof came out the same day.

Nvidia's troubles deepen: Reuters says the SEC probe now covers its accounting, and the stock fell about 13%. California's AG subpoenaed the company over possible chip diversion to China, and the AI sell-off pushed the Nasdaq negative for 2026 (Micron -13%, SoftBank -14.5%, KOSPI -5.2%).

Trump threatened a 'tremendous tax' on US firms building data centers abroad, naming Google's ~€13B Finland plan. In China, Tencent open-sourced its full 770B-parameter Hy4 MoE as Hang Seng Tech fell 3.78%.

items.title: Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis; Lean proof not yet independently checked
items.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note on Nov 20 saying he believes he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. He says the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Instead of a conventional paper he released a formal proof in Lean, split into a 14-part archive, along with a timeline he says Claude assembled (reportedly covering Oct 6 to Nov 16). Some preliminary technical details have been checked by others, but nobody has yet replayed and accepted the full formal proof. The same day, AMS president Ravi Vakil circulated a separate, 'all human' proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, which Brian Conrad has been reviewing for months.
items.why_it_matters: If the Lean proof checks out, it would be the first resolution of a Millennium Prize problem with major AI involvement, and a test of machine-checked proofs as a replacement for human refereeing. The rival human proof released the same day makes questions of priority and credit unavoidable.

items.title: Trump threatens a 'tremendous tax' on US firms that build data centers abroad, singling out Google's Finland plan

items.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over possible chip diversion to China and whether it misled investors
items.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Nov 19. The state Department of Justice is examining whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information reached China, whether the company misled investors and the public, and whether it broke state law. The probe follows reports about former CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. A subpoena is a fact-gathering step and carries no charge.
items.why_it_matters: A state investigation now sits alongside the SEC probe and several congressional inquiries, which widens Nvidia's legal exposure while it is under interim leadership and has held back its 10-Q.

items.title: Apollo and Goldman price $44B SpaceX GPU financing, the largest AI-chip debt deal, at yields above 8%
items.summary: Apollo and Goldman Sachs priced a roughly $44B debt package to fund SpaceX's purchase of Nvidia chips. Reuters reports the firms call it the largest AI-related chip financing ever arranged, and it was upsized on demand. The largest tranche, $25.17B of senior secured A3 notes due April 2033, priced at 8.259%. About $4.4B of A2 notes due 2031 priced at 7.66% and $2.564B of subordinated notes at 8.36%. items.why_it_matters: Investors demanded more than 8% yields, against about 5.95% on average investment-grade debt. That premium prices in the risk of GPU-backed, off-balance-sheet funding, which is becoming a template for AI capex.

items.title: Google adds Tool Retrieval to the Gemini API, loading tool schemas only when an agent needs them
items.summary: Google introduced Tool Retrieval in preview in the Gemini Interactions API for Gemini 3.6 and later models, including all Gemini 4 models. Developers add a tool_search tool and mark tools defer_loading: true. Only names and descriptions stay in context, and Google fetches a full parameter schema when the model asks for it, with no developer-hosted embedding index. Google's example: a 150-tool agent falls from 240,000 input tokens to about 19,800. There is no separate fee.
items.why_it_matters: Large tool catalogs, such as MCP servers and enterprise connectors, consume much of the context window. Google is following Anthropic's tool search and making on-demand tool loading a standard API feature, which cuts cost and tool-selection errors for big agents.

items.summary: OpenAI added GPT-Live-1.1, its full-duplex voice model, to the API along with a standby mode. On WebRTC sessions configured with wake_policy and idle_timeout_s (5-60 s), idle time is billed at $0.02 a minute against $0.05 for active inference, about 60% cheaper. items.why_it_matters: Billing for idle time has been a major cost in always-on voice agents. A cheaper hold state makes long open sessions, such as companions, call-center co-pilots and devices like Dots, cheaper to run.

learn.title: A formal checker certifies the stated theorem; audit the statement separately
learn.why_today: Alpöge released his Claude-assisted Riemann claim as a Lean proof, outlets disagree on whether it covers RH or GRH, and nobody has yet replayed the whole proof. Those are the two separate questions any machine-checked result raises: does it check, and is the checked statement the one claimed?
learn.explanation: A proof assistant's kernel guarantees that the proof term inhabits the formal statement, assuming the axioms and the kernel are sound. It says nothing about whether that statement, together with every definition it depends on, means what the English claim says. Errors hide in definitions (a mis-specified zeta function, a wrong domain), in dropped hypotheses, or in an added axiom or 'sorry' that the checker accepts. The same split runs through agent and LLM evaluation: a passing unit-test suite or grader certifies the spec it encodes, and a weak spec lets wrong answers through, which is reward hacking under another name. In practice, review the statement and its definitions by hand, list the axioms used (Lean's #print axioms), and test the spec against deliberately bad 'proofs' that it ought to reject. The toy below shows a dropped divisibility condition letting a nonsense witness verify.

learn.title: MoE sizing: memory follows total parameters, compute follows active ones
learn.why_today: Tencent's open Hy4 is reported as a MoE with about 770B total and 49B active parameters, a 15.7x gap that sets what hardware you need to serve it.
learn.explanation: In a mixture-of-experts layer a router sends each token to k of E expert FFNs, so the forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per active parameter, the same as a dense model of the active size. Every expert must still sit in memory, because the next token may route anywhere, so weight memory scales with total parameters. Decode at small batch is bound by memory bandwidth: each step reads the active experts' weights, so latency tracks active bytes. As batch size grows, tokens spread over more experts until a step touches nearly all of them, and serving cost moves toward the dense-total regime. That trade-off is why MoE is cheap per token at scale but needs many GPUs, or expert offloading, just to load the model. The numbers below are illustrative and ignore KV cache, activations and parallelism overheads.
learn.math: \text{FLOPs/token} \approx 2N_{active}, \qquad M_{weights} = N_{total}\, b, \qquad t_{decode} \gtrsim \frac{\min(N_{total},\, B N_{active})\, b}{BW}
learn.python:
# MoE: memory scales with TOTAL parameters, per-token compute with ACTIVE ones.
# Illustrative numbers only, using the reported 770B total / 49B active split.
total, active = 770e9, 49e9
dense_equiv = 49e9

for name, bytes_per_param in [("BF16", 2), ("FP8", 1), ("INT4", 0.5)]:
    weights_gb = total * bytes_per_param / 1e9
    gpus_80gb = weights_gb / 80
    print(f"{name}: weights {weights_gb:,.0f} GB -> at least {gpus_80gb:.1f} x 80GB GPUs just to hold them")

flops_per_token = 2 * active          # forward pass ~ 2 FLOPs per active parameter
print(f"forward FLOPs/token ~ {flops_per_token:.2e} (same as a {dense_equiv/1e9:.0f}B dense model)")
print(f"memory/compute ratio vs a 49B dense model: {total/active:.1f}x more weight bytes per FLOP")

# Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: at batch 1 each token must read the active experts' weights.
bw = 3.35e12                           # bytes/s, illustrative HBM bandwidth per GPU
for batch in (1, 32):
    bytes_read = min(total, active * batch)  # FP8 bytes; worst case: tokens spread over different experts
    print(f"batch {batch}: ~{bytes_read/1e9:,.0f} GB of expert weights touched per step "
          f"-> {bytes_read/bw*1e3:.1f} ms on one GPU's bandwidth")
